newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - ICICI, KEXIM, EBRD issues out.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - ICICI, KEXIM, EBRD issues out.

text.p: Asian debt markets gave what they promised on Thursday, with a number of issues expected to launch today doing just that.
Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India, better known as ICICI, launched its US$100 million step-up subordinated bond issue via lead managers SBC Warburg and Citibank International.
The notes have a final maturity of 10 years but can be called on the fifth anniversary.
They pay a margin of 80 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate for the first five years and the coupon steps up to 200 basis points in years six through 10 if the call is not exercised.
Fees are a sturdy 60 basis points, but SBC Warburg did not divulge the fee breakdown between management and underwriting and selling.
Syndicate managers in Hong Kong complained that the pricing of the issue is too tight for subordinated Indian paper.
"India is a mixed bag. We do see investor inquiries for Indian paper at reasonable spreads," said one manager.
"But for the policy banks like ICICI there is a lot of pressure to get into the deals for relationship purposes," he said.
Merrill Lynch presented Industrial Bank of India's seven-year straight FRN to investors in Singapore today and will take the roadshow to Hong Kong on Friday.
The Export-Import Bank of Korea, better known as Kexim, launched its US$500 million global bond through lead manager Lehman Brothers.
The bond matures in 10 years but can be put after five. It will be priced to yield 50-53 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasury bonds.

Bankers said the issue is expected to appeal to U.S. investors, which would regard the put option as insurance against a rising interest rate environment. "European investors also like puts but are not willing to pay for them," remarked one banker.
Bankers also pointed out that Korean paper has found U.S. investors more welcoming than investors elsewhere in the wake of the country's financial problems.

South Korea's central bank, seeking to calm fears that the second big corporate collapse this year could spur a banking crisis, today denied that Korea First Bank, the major creditor of both Hanbo and Sammi steel companies, was in trouble.
"Korea First Bank has no funding problem at all despite Sammi," said Park Chui, director of the central bank's monetary policy division.
Richard Samuelson, branch manager and head of research at SBC Warburg in Seoul, said that more South Korean companies could face bankruptcies this year.
He predicted that many of the same banks that had large exposures to Hanbo and Sammi will be shown to be lenders to other troubled companies as well.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see these same names in the banking sector crop up," Samuelson told Reuters Financial Television in its weekly Asian Debt Briefing.

"Our biggest concern is with Korea First Bank, it's a bank we've had a sell on for some time...but Commercial Bank of Korea and Korea Exchange Bank remain worrisome as well in terms of exposure to all of the questionable chaebols," he said.
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development launched its 2.0 billion peso one-year Eurobond. The 9.00 percent paper was priced at par and re-offered at 100.85.
In other news, Union Bank of Switzerland declined comment on widespread rumours that it is the winner of the Tenaga Yankee bond mandate.
